title: Chapter 20 – Behind the Founder's Tablet
html:
The paper is the hard part.

Lin Jian learns that in the first hour, standing in the burned-out corner of the library with a rag over his mouth and the ruin of the second shelf around his boots. The roof has been patched since the storm, with fresh gray tiles that do not match the old ones, and the smell of wet ash still lies in the air like a bad memory. Ten years of Wenhai's ledgers are pulp. The deed tube is gone. And there is nothing on the floor, nothing on the shelves, nothing in the whole dead room that could make a single sheet of anything look a hundred and fifty years old.

Except the books.

Grandfather's ancestors, on the farthest shelf, are slightly out of the rain's reach, and Lin Jian has found among them a volume of poems that nobody has opened in decades. It is a thin thing in a brown hemp cover, full of the sort of verse a young Lin Shoucheng might have written when he was still a wandering swordsman with water on his mind and no hill to call his own. The ink on its pages has faded to the color of tea. The binding has loosened. And at the front and back there are blank flyleaves, four of them, thick and soft and dry as a dead leaf.

Old-mill hemp, he thinks. The same hand-made stock, from the same decade, from the same river valley. The best match I will ever find.

He tears them out with a steady hand and a small shame, and carries them out through the broken door under his tunic.

* * *

He takes three more things that day.

The first is pine soot, a thumb-sized lump scraped from the underside of Father's inkstone, where it has gathered for twenty years from the lamp Father writes by. It is not the same as the soot Lin Shoucheng would have used, but pine soot is pine soot, and the one thing the interface cannot do is invent chemistry that does not exist.

The second is vermilion seal paste, a pinch from the family seal pot in the council room, which has sat on the same shelf since the day the first chop was made. It is not the same paste. It is a close cousin, dried and re-wetted a hundred times.

The third is nothing at all. It is a memory.

He sits on a sack of barley in the barred granary, in the afternoon, with the shutters closed and a Clear Light chip glowing on a nail, and he opens a door in the back of his head that he has not touched for six years. Three years old, in the old library, on the second shelf. A lacquered tube with a brass cap. A small boy who has just learned that if he looks at a thing hard enough, the whole world around it goes quiet, and every grain of it falls into place.

The cap had come off easily. The scroll inside had been hemp, thick and soft and old, with a square red seal in one corner and a second, round, in the other. He had looked at it for four minutes, because four minutes was the whole of his attention at that age. And then Second Uncle's footstep had come down the hall, and the boy had put the cap back and walked away.

The blueprint is still there. He knew that. He had put it away like a cloak in a cupboard, and he takes it out now, and shakes it, and holds it to the light.

```
[Blueprint — Land Deed, Hill Called Green Pine]
Captured: age 3y 2m, library, second shelf
Surface map: full (ink, seals, fibers, stains)
Fidelity: 99.7%
Required: Level 2 Fabrication
Materials needed: hemp sheet (aged), carbon pigment, cinnabar paste
Substitution check: aged hemp flyleaf, pine soot, family seal paste — ACCEPTABLE
Qi cost: 2.85 (capacity 5.10)
```

He reads it three times.

Fidelity: ninety-nine point seven. Not a copy. A reconstruction, grain by grain, of an object he saw once as a baby. It is a number that frightens him more than any number he has seen since the cave.

This is a forgery.

The thought comes cold and plain. He lets it. He has been honest with himself since the day he woke up in a body that had no business holding him, and he will not lie to himself about this.

It is also the only way to put back what was stolen.

He sits with both thoughts, and neither of them moves.

The deed was real. The hill was registered. The magistrate's seal was the magistrate's. A hundred and fifty years ago, a man with a sword and a bad leg dug a channel from a spring to a hillside and paid the county to write down that the water was his. That paper was taken in the night by a man the family trusted. If the family cannot show it, an arbiter who loves records will give the water to the people who stole them. And Lin Jian, by an accident of birth and a fact about his head that nobody else in the world shares, is the only living person who knows exactly what the paper said.

It is not a lie, he decides. It is a restoration.

It is a good argument. He is aware that it is the kind of argument a clever person makes to excuse a thing he has already decided to do. He puts it away, with the other debts, and picks up the flyleaf.

* * *

The fabrication takes the whole of one night.

It is not like the pins. A pin is a rod of iron with a groove. This is something finer, closer to growing than making, and the interface will not let him rush it. He sets the four flyleaves together on a board, one atop another, with the pine soot and the red paste in two chipped saucers at his elbow. He lays his left hand flat on the paper, and with his right he holds a hair of his own Qi like a thread, and he thinks the first word.

Build.

```
[Fabrication — Land Deed]
Stage 1: fuse substrate (4 leaves -> 1 sheet)
Stage 2: age profile (150 y, dry storage, tube-sealed)
Stage 3: surface print (ink, seals, stains)
Stage 4: residue check
Qi draw: 2.85 / 5.10
Warning: sustained draw above 2.0 will cause exhaustion
```

The four leaves lift. They do not move, exactly. They settle, the way sand settles in water, fibers sliding between fibers until the seams close and there is only one sheet, a little yellower than before, a little more brittle at the edges. Then the surface begins to darken.

It starts at the corners. A faint brown stain, like old tea. A crease where a scroll was rolled too tightly. Then the characters, rising from the paper rather than falling on it, as though the fibers themselves were remembering what they had once held. Land Deed of the Hill Called Green Pine, Registered by Lin Shoucheng. A formal paragraph in the stiff, square hand of a county clerk. And below it, in smaller, rougher strokes, the way a soldier writes when he has been handed a brush and does not trust it:

The spring, and the channel I cut from it. Lin water, by my sword and my sweat.

He reads that line three times with the lamp guttering, and something tightens behind his eyes that has nothing to do with Qi.

The seals come last. The square one, red and thick, in the lower left. Lin Shoucheng. And the round county mark in the upper right, broken at the edge where the stamp had been cracked, a flaw he remembers because it had annoyed his three-year-old mind.

By the fourth hour he is shaking. By the sixth, the sweat has soaked through his tunic. The Qi draw is not much by the standards of a cultivator, but he has never held it for so long, and by the seventh hour his vision is going gray at the edges. He sets his teeth. He keeps the thread steady.

Stage 4.

```
[Residue Check]
Foreign Qi trace: 0.31% (QR5, wood-earth)
Source: operator
Risk: spiritual sense above Foundation stage may detect operator signature
Recommended: SEPARATE operator Qi from fibers
Cost: 2 CE (remaining: 114 / 400)
```

He has not thought of that. He has thought of the ink and the paper and the seals, and the dozen small ways a clever eye might see that this was one night old. He has not thought of himself. A man who looks at a sheet of hemp does not see the hand that made it, but an arbiter who has judged border disputes for sixty years has a mind that is a kind of hand, and it would feel the warmth of a living boy in the grain like a thumbprint in wax.

Separate.

The trace lifts out of the fibers as a faint gray haze, like breath on cold glass, and fades. The sheet lies still. It looks, now, exactly like what it is meant to be: a land deed that has lain in a lacquered tube in a dry library for a hundred and fifty years, with nobody's hand on it.

He releases the thread, and the room goes sideways, and he slides down the sack of barley and sleeps for fourteen hours.

* * *

He wakes to the sound of Kai's knuckles on the shutter and the taste of copper in his mouth.

"Cousin?" The voice is low and urgent. "It's past noon. Your mother says if you're not up by dark she's going to break the door."

"Tell her I'm up."

"Are you?"

"No."

He is lying on the granary floor with his cheek on a barley sack and his hair full of chaff. His hands tremble when he lifts them. But the deed is there, on the board beside his head, rolled and pale, with the lamp stub burned out above it. He touches the corner with one finger. The paper is dry, and slightly rough, and has the slightly sweet smell of old hemp in a closed room.

He sits up and eats the whole of the cold millet cake Kai pushes through the shutter. Then he wraps the deed in a scrap of oilcloth, as it would have been wrapped, a hundred and fifty years ago, by a man with no sense of the future, and goes to find a place to put it.

* * *

The ancestral hall stands behind the main house, a small, dark building with a low roof and a smell of old incense, and its doors have never been locked in the memory of anyone living. It does not need to be. No Lin would enter it without cause, and no thief would think of it.

Inside, six generations wait in rows.

They are plain tablets, tall slabs of black wood with gold-leaf names, each one on its own stand. The newer ones have simple turned feet. The older ones have carved bases of pines and cranes. And at the back, on a dais of one step, under a small round window that lets in a single shaft of dusty light, stands the tablet of Lin Shoucheng.

It is the oldest, the largest, and the plainest. The wood has gone to the color of dark honey. There are no cranes, no gold. Only a name, and under it a date. But the stand is another matter. It is hollow, a boxy frame of black wood carved with pine branches, deeper than it looks, and at the back, between the third and fourth branch, there is a gap about the width of two fingers.

Lin Jian found it at the age of four, when he was taken to the hall for the first time and lost interest in the incense. Nobody else has ever noticed. He has not told anyone.

He comes in the first hour of night, after the evening offering, when the last uncle has bowed and gone and the lamps in the front hall have been put out. A single stick of incense is burning in the ash before the founder's tablet. He stands before it and bows three times, because it is what a Lin child does, and because he means it.

Then he walks around the stand, and slides the oilcloth bundle into the gap, and presses it deep until it falls out of sight into the hollow beneath the branches with a faint, dry scrape.

It is done in thirty seconds. It is a great deal less than the weight in his hands.

He stands there for a moment longer in the dark. Somewhere behind the wall, a lamp is lit. A footstep goes by outside. The incense stick burns down to a red point and flickers.

"I am sorry, Grandfather," he whispers to the tablet of a man he never met. "I do not think you would have approved. I think you would have understood."

Then he goes out into the night, and the door closes softly behind him.

* * *

The tablets get their spring cleaning on the third morning.

It is an old custom, the week of the sweeping of graves. Every family in the valley cleans its dead, and the Lins do it as they do everything, without fuss. Old Nan, who has led the cleaning for forty years, comes in at dawn with a bundle of white cloths and a bucket of well water, and the younger women of the household come behind her carrying brooms.

Lin Jian arrives with Lin Yue.

He has not planned it. His sister attaches herself to his hand at breakfast, as she often does, and by the time they reach the hall door she is talking about spiders. He told her the day before, offhandedly, that there were enormous ones in the old hall, behind the founder's stand, big as her palm, with hairy legs. He regrets it a little now, watching her face. But it was the right thing to say.

"You said they'd be big," Yue says, from behind his shoulder.

"I said they might be."

"I want to see one."

"Then stay with Old Nan and do not touch anything."

She is six. She does exactly the opposite. Old Nan is dusting the third row, her brown hands moving in the slow, even arcs of long habit. Two aunts are on their knees at the side wall with their buckets. A Dust-Away talisman is pasted to the lintel, glowing faintly green, drawing the grime off the old beams in a thin gray veil that settles into a bag. It is Lin Yue's sandals, scuffing across the boards, that carry her to the dais; and it is Lin Yue's small fingers, reaching into the gap between the third branch and the fourth, that close on a cold, rough bundle of oilcloth and pull.

"Brother," she says, in a very interested voice. "There isn't a spider. There's a parcel."

The hall goes quiet.

Old Nan's cloth stops in mid-stroke. One of the aunts says, "Yue, put that down," and then, because she has turned her head and seen the shape of it, says nothing more.

Lin Yue puts it down. She puts it down very gently, in both hands, on the top step of the dais, because it is the kind of thing that wants to be put down gently. And Lin Jian, standing by the door with his face smooth and his heart going like a hammer, steps forward, and says in a perfectly ordinary voice, "I think someone should get Grandfather."

* * *

Grandfather arrives at a walk that is nearly a run.

He has not run in thirty years. He stops at the foot of the dais, breathing hard, with his hand on the stand of the nearest tablet, and looks at the bundle on the step. Nobody speaks. The shaft of light from the high window lies across the oilcloth like a finger.

He kneels. It takes him a long time. When he is down, he reaches out with a hand that is not entirely steady and unwraps the cloth, fold by fold, until the roll of pale hemp lies in his palm. He opens it a hand's width.

He reads.

Lin Jian watches his face. He has watched it for nine years, and he has seen it angry and tired and amused, and he has seen it grieve. He has never seen this. It does not break. It simply opens, the way a locked door opens when the right key is turned, and all the weight of forty years goes out of it at once.

"He made two," Grandfather says.

The words are very soft. They are not addressed to anyone in the room.

"You cunning old wolf. You made two."

A tear runs down the side of his nose and drops into the white of his beard. He does not wipe it. He kneels there before the tablet of the man who dug the channel, with the deed on his open palm, and he laughs, once, a short broken sound, and then he is crying openly, in front of the aunts and Old Nan and a six-year-old girl who looks very pleased with herself.

The family will talk about it for years. They will tell each other how Lin Shoucheng, the stubborn old swordsman, made a copy of his deed and hid it where only a child would find it, as a gift to a family he would never meet. It will become the best story in the Hollow. Lin Jian will hear it told at weddings, and funerals, and once by Third Aunt to a stranger on the road, and every time he will listen with a face of perfect, grave interest.

Across the hall, in the doorway, Second Uncle stands motionless.

Lin Jian does not look at him directly. He does not need to. He sees it from the corner of his eye: the face gone the color of candle wax, the lips parting, a single soundless word forming on them. He has learned to read mouths since Hu started teaching him to watch for the tells of a fighter. This one is not hard.

Impossible.

Then Wenhai's expression smooths. He comes forward one step and bows, deeply, to the old man kneeling at the dais. "A blessing from the ancestors," he says, in a voice that is almost steady. "The Lins are fortunate." He turns, and walks out through the door, and the sunlight swallows him.

He does not come to dinner.

* * *

The arbiter arrives on foot.

He comes up the valley road at midmorning on the fourth day, with a small cloth bundle over one shoulder and a staff of plain dark wood, and he stops to drink from the stream before he enters the gate. Grandfather has gathered the whole family at the entrance to greet him: forty-one Lins in their best clothes, shifting from foot to foot in the cold. A flying boat would have been easier. The Outer Affairs Hall owns three.

"A man who arrives on a flying boat," Hu murmurs at Lin Jian's shoulder, "has already decided he is above the ground. This one walked."

Shen Wuye is not tall. He looks perhaps fifty, though Lin Jian's sense tells him the real figure is older by two or three times. His beard is square and gray, trimmed to a precise edge; his robe is plain gray cotton, spotted with road dust. He has the face of a man who has listened to sixty years of liars, and has not become bitter, only careful.

His Qi is the first thing Lin Jian notices. It does not roll off him like Zhao Heng's, or glitter like Gu Yan's. It sits very quietly in his body, deep and settled, like a lake under ice. Mid-stage Foundation Establishment. He could, if he chose, crush the entire Hollow with a thought, and he is walking up the road on his own two feet with a dust-covered staff, as polite as a schoolmaster.

"Patriarch Lin," Shen says, and bows exactly as deeply as a man of his rank should bow to a man of Grandfather's, and not a hair more. "I have walked past your terraces. They are well kept."

"They are watered," Grandfather says, "by the thing we are here to discuss."

A flicker of dry humor crosses the gray face. "So I understand."

* * *

The hearing is held at the spring itself.

That is Shen's decision, announced on the road: he does not judge a water dispute in a room. He wishes to stand where the water stands. They climb the path behind the great terraces, a hundred and sixty people in a slow procession, Lins and Zhaos and villagers and a handful of clerks from Willow Ford, and arrive at a shelf of gray stone under two old pines.

The spring is smaller than Lin Jian remembered. A hand-wide cleft in the rock, with a trickle of clear cold water slipping out of it into a worn round basin. From the basin, a stone-lined channel leads away down the hill, as straight and neat as a ruler stroke. And above the cleft, scratched into the stone with the point of a blade, so old that the edges of the cut have gone smooth and gray, a single character:

Lin.

Zhao Heng stands on the other side of the basin.

He is lean and straight in a deep green robe with a stiff collar, his hair bound in a dark jade ring. He does not look like a man who has come to win a court case. He looks like a man who is attending the funeral of a distant relative. Beside him stands Zhao Qian, young and hard-faced, with the same cold stare, and four cultivators in the Zhao family colors. Behind them, on a bench, sit two very old villagers in their Sunday clothes.

Lin Jian watches the Foundation Establishment patriarch of Red Ridge, and the Foundation Establishment patriarch watches him back, once, for an instant, with the slow dull stare of a snake that has not yet decided to strike. Then Zhao Heng looks away.

He knows.

It is not a thought. It is a cold feeling, spreading from the base of Lin Jian's skull. Zhao Heng knows something he is not saying. He knows it the way a man knows he has locked his door.

* * *

The Zhao case takes an hour.

It is not a bad one. A survey, signed and sealed, commissioned by Zhao Heng's grandfather, which places the head of the spring a hundred paces east of the line the Lins claim. Two witnesses who swear that in their fathers' time the water had been shared. A neat map, a neat voice, a neat argument. Shen listens to all of it without moving, his staff planted before him, his eyes half closed.

"The survey is dated?" he says.

"The fourteenth year of the reign," says Zhao Heng's clerk.

"And the Lin claim?"

"They have a deed," says Grandfather.

He stands, and he takes the scroll from the oilcloth, and he walks across the stone to the arbiter and offers it on both palms, like a man giving up his son. His hands, Lin Jian notes, are perfectly steady.

Shen takes it. He does not unroll it at once. He closes his eyes, and Lin Jian feels something settle over the shelf of stone, a pressure in the air, like the moment before thunder. The old man's spiritual sense. It moves across the paper in a slow wave, and Lin Jian's heart stops.

The residue. The seals. The age.

He has done everything. He has stripped his own Qi from the fibers. He has aged the sheet to the century and a half. He has matched the soot to the hemp. And he thinks of everything he has not thought of, all the ways of the world he cannot see, and the cold thought comes again: he is a Foundation Establishment elder. He has read ten thousand deeds. Of course he will know.

The pressure lifts.

Shen opens his eyes. He unrolls the scroll with the unhurried care of a man who has handled a lot of old paper, holds it up to the light, and reads aloud, in a clear dry voice, the lines at the bottom.

"The spring, and the channel I cut from it. Lin water, by my sword and my sweat."

Silence.

"Old-mill hemp," says Shen Wuye, quietly, to himself. "A hundred and fifty years, give or take. Pine soot. A genuine county seal. The crack in the stamp matches the registry copy at Willow Ford." He looks up. "This is a good deed."

Nobody breathes.

"The survey of the Zhao family," he says, turning to Zhao Heng, "was commissioned ten years after this deed was registered. A later survey cannot unmake an earlier deed. If your grandfather moved the line, he moved it by ten years too late." His voice is dry and gentle. "The water is Lin water. By deed, by use, and by sword."

He raps the butt of his staff once on the stone.

It is not loud. It is final.

* * *

The Lin family does not cheer. They are not a cheering family. But a long sound goes through them, a sort of collective exhale, and then the aunts are weeping and the cousins are hugging, and Old Gou, who is eighty, has sat down on a rock with his hat over his face and is laughing into it. Father's hand finds Lin Jian's shoulder and squeezes once, hard. Mother does not touch him. She stands a few paces away with her arms folded, looking at the cleft in the rock, and her face is quiet and unreadable and very proud.

Lin Jian sits down on a stone.

He is eight years old, and nearly nine. He has just stood in front of an elder of the Azure Cloud Sect, with a forged deed in his family's hands, and he has not once been caught. He feels sick. He feels as if he has swallowed a stone, and the stone is sitting in the pit of his chest, cool and heavy, and he knows with perfect clarity that it is going to be there for a very long time.

Putting back what was stolen, he thinks.

It is a good argument. It is still a good argument.

He looks up.

Zhao Heng is walking away.

He walks the way a man walks who has lost nothing. His back is straight, his steps are even, and he does not look at the arbiter, or at Grandfather, or at the rock with the scratched character. He walks down toward the path with Zhao Qian and the four cultivators behind him, and as he passes the line of Lin retainers, he comes level with Second Uncle.

Wenhai is standing alone, a little apart from the others, his face blank, his arms hanging at his sides.

Zhao Heng does not stop. He does not slow. But his head turns very slightly, just enough that his eyes rest on the steward's face for the space of one heartbeat, and he says, in a voice pitched to carry exactly as far as one man:

"We will talk, Steward."

The patriarch of Red Ridge walks on. Behind him, the pines move softly in the wind, and Second Uncle stands where he is, turned to stone.

Lin Jian does not look at him. He looks at the water, running clear and cold down its neat straight channel into the terraces, and thinks about a locked chest in a house at Red Ridge, and a lacquered tube with a brass cap, and the one man in the valley who knows, to the last stroke of ink, exactly what is inside.

Zhao Heng knows the real deed is safe in his own house. And he cannot say a word.

It is a very quiet kind of victory. It is also, he understands, the end of something. The Zhao patriarch does not keep tools that turn in his hand.

Wenhai has lost his master's protection. And a man who has nothing left to lose is a man who may do anything.
